articles.title: Frostbite injuries in Refugees: Analysis of delayed presentation, amputation risk, and clinical outcomes.
articles.journal: Burns : journal of the International Society for Burn Injuries
articles.abstract: Frostbite injuries remain a significant clinical problem, particularly in populations exposed to harsh environmental conditions and limited access to healthcare. This study aimed to evaluate the clinical characteristics, risk factors, and outcomes of frostbite cases managed at a tertiary care center. This retrospective study included 159 patients diagnosed with frostbite over five years. Demographic, clinical, and laboratory data were recorded for all patients. Cases were classified according to frostbite severity. Statistical analyses were performed using SPSS software, with a significance threshold set at p < 0.05. The majority of patients were young males (97.5%), and a large proportion consisted of refugees. Most cases were classified as fourth-degree frostbite (77.4%). The overall amputation rate was 76.1%. The strongest predictors of amputation were higher frostbite grade (p < 0.001), hypotension at admission (p < 0.001), elevated white blood cell count (p = 0.006), and greater TBSA involvement (p = 0.040). Refugee status was also associated with increased amputation risk (p = 0.035). The mean hospital length of stay was 14.3 ± 7.3 days, which was higher than values reported in the literature, largely due to delayed hospital presentation. Frostbite injuries in this cohort were associated with high amputation rates. Delayed presentation and advanced-stage injuries appear to be the main drivers of poor clinical outcomes. Early presentation, prompt diagnosis, and timely initiation of appropriate treatment remain critical in reducing morbidity and improving overall outcomes.

articles.title: Acute dermal toxicity and wound healing effects of Salvia palaestina Benth. in vivo: Targeting inflammation, oxidative stress, and apoptosis.
articles.journal: Burns : journal of the International Society for Burn Injuries
articles.abstract: The study investigates acute dermal toxicity and wound healing effects of a traditional medicinal herb, Salvia palaestina Benth leaf extracts (SPLE), in the excisional wound model. Thirty-six SD rats for acute dermal toxicity were aligned into three cages (n = 12), and for the wound experiment, thirty rats were wounded on their dorsal necks and aligned randomly into five groups (n = 6), treated with saline (untreated), 10% Tween 20 (blank), intrasite gel (reference), 2.5% SPLE, or 5% SPLE for 15 days. The results demonstrated the non-toxic effects of topical SPLE application, while also accelerating wound contraction and reducing the inflammatory process. After 15 days of application, SPLE (2.5% and 5%) enhanced wound closure by 80.28% and 85.91%, respectively, relative to the initial wound size. The histopathological observation of SPLE (2.5% and 5%)-treated wound skin revealed increased re-epithelialization, increased hydroxyproline by 5.4, 3.5, and 4.1-fold, and more fibroblast deposition than untreated rats. SPLEs' anti-apoptotic (negatively modulating Bax protein) and cell proliferation effects (increasing PCNA expression) were linked with their promoting action on epidermal growth via diminishing cell death, keratinocyte proliferation/migration, and encouraging vascularization. Moreover, SPLE (2.5 and 5%)-treated rats showed reduced oxidative stress and inflammatory process, increasing SOD by 43.1, 123.9%; CAT by 139.7, 154.3%, along with lowering MDA by 16.9%, 38.8%, respectively. In parallel with lowering TNF-α by 50.1%, 68.9%; CRP by 41.6, 47.7%; IL-6 by 50.7, 61.3%, altogether promoting a balanced, faster wound recovery. In conclusion, SPLE exhibited a non-toxic and pro-healing effect, modulating several cellular processes, which make it a viable therapeutic source for wound management.

articles.title: Bandages & Brews: Evaluation of an Open-Access Community Wilderness Medicine Education Intervention.
articles.abstract: IntroductionOutdoor recreation in the Pacific Northwest frequently exposes individuals to wilderness environments where delays to definitive care can increase morbidity and mortality. Limited access to formal wilderness medicine training may contribute to preventable emergencies. We developed Bandages & Brews, a free community-based wilderness medicine event designed to improve preparedness among recreational participants.MethodsBandages & Brews was held in Portland, Oregon, in March 2026. Participants rotated through four hands-on stations: first aid kits and trail logistics, splinting, bleeding control, and head injury assessment. Curriculum was based on Wilderness Medical Society guidelines, International Commission for Alpine Rescue recommendations, and Auerbach's Wilderness Medicine. Outcomes were assessed using retrospective pre-post surveys, objective skill assessments, and 60-day follow-up surveys.ResultsMore than 50 individuals attended; 35 completed retrospective pre-post surveys and 24 completed 60-day follow-up. Participants demonstrated significant improvements across all confidence domains (p < 0.001), with the largest gains in splinting and hemorrhage control. Preparedness behaviors, including carrying first aid supplies and emergency communication devices, also improved significantly. Most improvements were sustained at 60 days, with additional gains in confidence regarding head injury assessment and evacuation decisions. Confidence moderately correlated with objective performance (rho = 0.433, p = 0.083). Participants universally reported positive experiences.ConclusionsBandages & Brews is a feasible, low-barrier model for community wilderness medicine education associated with sustained improvements in confidence and preparedness behaviors. Community-based experiential programs may represent an underutilized public health approach to promoting safer outdoor recreation.

articles.title: Dark Urine After Nonfatal Drowning: Rhabdomyolysis-Associated Acute Kidney Injury and Freshwater Aspiration Pneumonia.
articles.abstract: Nonfatal drowning is managed primarily as a respiratory emergency, but clinically important kidney injury may be overlooked, particularly with delayed presentation. A previously healthy 53-y-old man fell into a freshwater pond that may have been contaminated by wastewater, struggled for ∼30 to 60 min, aspirated water, and presented 2 to 3 d later with fever, dyspnea, oliguria, and dark brown urine. Respiratory testing identified Aeromonas hydrophila complex and Escherichia coli, supporting drowning-associated pneumonia after freshwater aspiration. Serum creatinine was 986 μmol·L-1 (11.2 mg·dL-1), creatine kinase 79,765 U·L-1, and serum myoglobin 8630 ng·mL-1; urine was heme positive with few red blood cells. The patient had Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes stage 3 acute kidney injury requiring continuous renal replacement therapy followed by intermittent hemodialysis. Dialysis ended on Day 25, and kidney function normalized by Day 94. Delayed presentation, prolonged struggle, hypoxemia, oliguria, and dark urine should prompt targeted renal assessment after drowning. When drowning-associated pneumonia is evident clinically, respiratory sampling should guide antimicrobial treatment; renal replacement therapy should be used for standard severe acute kidney injury indications rather than myoglobin removal alone.

articles.title: Preparedness of Backcountry Recreationists in the Sea to Sky Corridor, British Columbia, Canada.
articles.abstract: IntroductionThe Sea to Sky Corridor in British Columbia, Canada, is home to highly trafficked backcountry terrain with frequent Search and Rescue (SAR) incidents. Recreationist preparedness is an important factor to help reduce incidents. This study analyzed the preparedness of winter and summer recreationists in the Sea to Sky Corridor.MethodsPreviously collected anonymized data from Squamish SAR trailhead outreach conducted during the summer and winter of 2022-2023 were analyzed. Groups were interviewed, and their demographics and preparedness were assessed. Preparedness was summarized using a composite score (0-13) based on key elements, which included carrying the Ten Essentials, route research, checking the weather, leaving a trip plan, and emergency knowledge. Winter groups also were assessed for avalanche safety practices. Mean preparedness scores were compared between seasons and training using independent t tests.ResultsA total of 123 groups (summer n=81; winter n=42) were included. Summer groups were exclusively hikers, whereas winter groups were predominantly backcountry skiers/splitboarders. Mean preparedness scores were significantly higher in winter than in summer (10.04±3.59 vs 7.05±2.59; P<0.0001). No summer group carried all Ten Essentials, whereas 48% of winter groups did. Although most winter groups (88%) had avalanche training, approximately one quarter did not check the forecast and one quarter carried incomplete avalanche setups. No snowshoeing groups carried avalanche equipment, and three quarters had no training.ConclusionsPreparedness gaps were identified across both cohorts, particularly among summer hikers and winter snowshoers. These findings highlight clear targets for prevention strategies in the Sea to Sky Corridor.

articles.title: High Altitude Hypothermia Reversal in the Field: A Case from Northern Pakistan, Karakoram Range.
articles.abstract: Severe accidental hypothermia is a well-recognized risk in high altitude environments, where sudden weather changes, prolonged exposure to unstable temperatures, and limited medical access can rapidly become life threatening. In remote areas such as the Karakoram Range of northern Pakistan, improvised rewarming techniques may be the only viable option until evacuation is possible. We report a case of a 32-y-old healthy male trekker who was found unresponsive by his companions at ∼4200 m in the Karakoram Range with a recorded axillary temperature of 27°C, measured using a portable low-reading thermometer (Braun digital). At the time of discovery, the estimated ambient temperature was approximately -10°C with sustained winds of 15 to 20 km/h, contributing to significant cold exposure. The patient was bradycardic with a heart rate of 32 beats/min, hypotensive with blood pressure of 70/40 mmHg, respiratory rate of 8 breaths/min, and unconscious with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 6/15 (E1 V1 M4). On assessment, he was cold to touch with rigid extremities and weak peripheral pulses, findings consistent with moderate to severe hypothermia. He was initially unresponsive and then only responded to stimulation by groaning. Because of delayed access to formal medical care, the trekking team initiated field rewarming using improvised methods such as heated rocks wrapped in cloth applied to axillae and groin, insulation with multiple clothing layers and foil blankets, and intermittent truncal body-to-body contact. Over a few hours, his temperature increased to 34°C. He became alert and oriented to person and place, with heart rate rising to ∼60 beats/min, blood pressure improving to ∼100/60 mm Hg, and respiratory rate normalizing to 16 breaths/min. The team subsequently evacuated him to a local medical facility, where he recovered fully without neurologic deficits. This case demonstrates that simple physiology-based rewarming measures can be effective in reversing hypothermia when advanced equipment is unavailable. Early insulation with active external rewarming can be effective in treating hypothermia in austere settings. We recommend basic cold injury training for trekking teams.

articles.title: Shark Bites in Florida Are Underreported: A Multi-Dataset Analysis.
articles.abstract: IntroductionThere is uncertainty about the number of shark bites on humans in Florida (FL).MethodsThe International Shark Attack File (ISAF) and Global Shark Attack File (GSAF) databases (2016-2024) were compared with the non-inpatient FL Ambulatory and Emergency Department Patient Data database (AHCA) (2018-2023) and the National Emergency Medical Services (EMS) Information System (NEMSIS) (2016-2024).ResultsBetween 2016-2024 there were 244 FL shark encounters reported in ISAF (mean 27.1 per year), 214 in GSAF (mean 23.8 per year), and 293 in a merged ISAF and GSAF (mean 32.6 per year). Between 2020-2023, there were 373 FL shark encounters reported in AHCA (mean 62.2 per year) compared with 114 encounters reported in NEMSIS (mean 22.8 per year) for 2020-2024. The rate ratio for AHCA FL shark encounters compared to the merged ISAF and GSAF was 1.91 (95% CI 1.64-2.23); p < .001. The percentage of shark encounters in Volusia County, FL, compared with all of FL shark encounters showed no significant differences between the ISAF and GSAF (40.2% and 33.6%, respectively) (p = .16) and between the AHCA and NEMSIS (7.2% and 7.5%, respectively) (p = 1.0). However, when comparing either ISAF or GSAF with either AHCA or NEMSIS, there were significant differences (p < .001 for all).DiscussionThe AHCA dataset identified about twice as many shark bites as either the ISAF or GSAF. Many FL shark encounters did not require EMS or admission to the hospital. The discrepancy in the number of shark encounters attributed to Volusia County, FL, varied based on the dataset being examined.

articles.title: ESR and CRP Testing in an Urban Emergency Department: Should We Still Be Doing This?
articles.abstract: Pediatricians in the Emergency Department frequently evaluate febrile children. To help identify the cause of fever and assess the severity of the underlying condition, practitioners often utilize erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein testing. While these markers of inflammation are deeply embedded in the practice of pediatrics, they were each developed more than 90 years ago, and their utility to current clinical practice is not well characterized. We conducted a 1-year retrospective study of children who underwent CRP and ESR testing at an urban Children's Hospital. We recorded and analyzed indications for testing, concordance between testing methods and metrics, including admission status and test performance, as reflected by sensitivity, specificity, and likelihood ratios. ESR and CRP tests were frequently ordered in patients with clinically evident diagnoses. There were no cases of occult bacteremia, and patients with bacteremia typically had presentations indicative of bacterial infection. CRP was superior to ESR as a predictor of bacterial infection; however, the positive likelihood ratio was only 2.1. Combined testing was ordered for 39.4% of all CRP tests, and there was a high concordance (69.9%) between CRP and ESR testing. Combined testing offered limited incremental value for the detection of bacterial infections. CRP and ESR testing are currently overused in our Pediatric Emergency Department, providing limited diagnostic value while adding unnecessary hospital cost. Combined CRP and ESR testing provides limited incremental value. Stewardship of these testing modalities and an active reconsideration of how these tests are employed should be considered.

articles.title: Anaphylaxis in Infants and Toddlers Presenting to a Pediatric Emergency Department.
articles.abstract: To characterize the clinical presentation and management of anaphylaxis in infants and toddlers. We conducted a retrospective cohort study of patients aged 0 to 24 months presenting to a pediatric emergency department between June 2019 and June 2022 with concern for anaphylaxis. Patients were identified using International Classification of Diseases, Ninth and 10th Revision codes associated with anaphylaxis and confirmed to meet 2006 National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases/Food Allergy and Anaphylaxis Network clinical criteria by chart review. Demographic and clinical information-including presenting symptoms, administered treatment, and patient disposition-were abstracted from the electronic medical record. Treatments of interest included epinephrine, antihistamines, corticosteroids, albuterol, and intravenous fluids. Data were analyzed descriptively. Among 225 potentially eligible encounters, we identified 155 patients who met inclusion criteria. Median age was 10.8 months (interquartile range: 8.4 to 15.6). Food triggered 96.1% of episodes. Skin and mucosal symptoms occurred in 99.4% of patients, gastrointestinal symptoms in 74.2%, respiratory symptoms in 57.4%, and cardiovascular symptoms in 5.8%. Intramuscular epinephrine was administered to 87.1% of patients, 90.4% of whom received a single dose. Most patients (88.4%) were discharged home, and none of those admitted required additional epinephrine. In this cohort, reactions were most often food-triggered and characterized by mucocutaneous symptoms with gastrointestinal and/or mild-to-moderate respiratory symptoms. Severe respiratory or cardiovascular involvement was uncommon. Symptoms tended to resolve after a single dose of epinephrine, and most patients were discharged home.

articles.title: Bystander AED Effectiveness Despite Low Utilisation in OHCA.
authors: Korean Cardiac Arrest Research Consortium (KoCARC) Investigators
articles.abstract: Observational estimates of bystander automated external defibrillator (AED) effectiveness are inconsistent in settings with mature public-access defibrillation infrastructure but low utilization, partly because the conventional reference group pools emergency medical services (EMS)-shocked with non-defibrillated patients. We estimated bystander AED effectiveness against a partitioned no-defibrillation reference, tested effect modification by location, and quantified the deployment-utilization gap. Retrospective analysis of a prospectively collected multicenter out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) registry (Korea, October 2015-June 2025; 23,918 adults of presumed medical etiology). A three-tier prehospital defibrillation-provider variable was defined: bystander AED applied (n = 383); EMS-delivered shock without preceding bystander AED (n = 5,975); and no prehospital defibrillation (reference; n = 17,560). Primary outcomes were survival to discharge and good neurological outcome (Cerebral Performance Category 1-2), analyzed by multivariable logistic regression with propensity-score, inverse-probability-weighting and location-stratified secondary analyses. Bystander AED application was associated with improved survival (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 1.60; 95% CI 1.19-2.14) and good neurological outcome (2.31; 1.65-3.23), comparable to that of EMS-delivered shock; the pooled-control specification attenuated estimates to non-significance (survival 1.09; neurological 1.14). Shock-delivered applications significantly exceeded EMS-delivered shock for neurological outcome (aOR 1.43; p = 0.03). Effectiveness did not differ by location (interaction p ≥ 0.15). Bystander AED was applied in 8.5% of Public-area versus 1.9% of Nonpublic AED-opportunity cases-a 4.5-fold gap. Bystander AED was associated with improved outcomes when applied, comparable to or exceeding EMS-delivered shock; the dominant constraint was the deployment-utilization gap, greatest in residential settings. Residential rapid-activation infrastructure warrants policy priority alongside, not instead of, continued device placement.

articles.title: Supporting Mental Health in EMS Clinicians: A NAEMSP Position Statement and Resource Document.
articles.abstract: Emergency medical services (EMS) clinicians operate in environments characterized by repeated trauma exposure, operational unpredictability, shift work, moral distress, and cumulative occupational stress. A substantial body of evidence demonstrates elevated rates of post-traumatic stress symptoms, depression, anxiety, substance use, sleep disturbance, burnout, and suicide among EMS clinicians and other public safety professionals compared to the general public. The implications extend beyond individual well-being, affecting workforce sustainability, clinical performance, and high quality patient care. Mental health in EMS is therefore not solely an individual concern, but a systems issue. Therefore, the National Association of EMS Physicians (NAEMSP) recommends that:Organizational leadership should recognize EMS clinician mental health as foundational to workforce sustainability and safe patient care.EMS clinician mental health awareness, management, and treatment options should be a core part of EMS education.EMS systems should take a multi-faceted approach to mental health, with an emphasis on ensuring access to confidential and culturally competent resources for EMS clinicians and other public safety professionals including telecommunicators, law enforcement officers and firefighters.EMS systems should engage in quality improvement to identify and improve practices affecting EMS clinician mental health.EMS systems should achieve meaningful and sustainable improvements in EMS clinician mental health through legislative advocacy and building strong partnerships with local, regional and national agencies including public health and research institutions.

articles.title: Consensus Guidelines for Prehospital Transfusion in Children: A Modified Delphi Study.
articles.abstract: Hemorrhagic shock is a leading cause of early trauma-related mortality in children, yet implementation of prehospital blood transfusion (PHT) in children is heterogenous and without consistent guidance. Limited pediatric-specific evidence and physiologic differences from adults have contributed to substantial variability among existing emergency medical services (EMS) protocols. The objective of this study was to develop expert consensus recommendations for identifying pediatric patients who may benefit from PHT. We conducted a modified Delphi consensus study using a multidisciplinary panel of 20 experts in pediatric surgery, pediatric emergency medicine, and EMS medicine. Investigators compiled candidate criteria from existing PHT protocols and expert input. We conducted iterative electronic surveys to achieve expert consensus. We predefined consensus thresholds as ≥80% agreement for inclusion and <50% for exclusion. We employed descriptive statistics to summarize responses across rounds. The panel evaluated 208 candidate items and accepted 35 recommendations for inclusion over six rounds of voting. Consensus defined eligibility for PHT in children consisting of (1) known or suspected severe hemorrhage or major blood loss, (2) at least one indicator of shock following first-line hemorrhage control, and (3) EMS clinical judgment of the need for transfusion. Shock indicators included physiologic compromise, hemodynamic instability, poor perfusion, low cardiac output, or an abnormal validated pediatric shock index. Contraindications included do not resuscitate orders prohibiting transfusion and non-hemorrhagic shock. We were unable to reach consensus on routine inclusion of end-tidal carbon dioxide as an indication for transfusion. Experts came to consensus on pediatric-focused, pragmatic criteria to guide prehospital blood product transfusion in children. Implementation of these recommendations may reduce practice variability, support protocol development, and inform future prospective validation studies.

articles.title: Clonal Hematopoiesis and Inflammatory Pathways in Heart Failure with Preserved Ejection Fraction.
articles.abstract: This review aims to examine the role of clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential (CHIP) in the pathophysiology of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), focusing on its contribution to inflammation, disease development, and clinical implications. Recent studies demonstrate that CHIP is enriched in HFpEF populations and is associated with increased disease risk and worse clinical outcomes. Mechanistically, CHIP promotes inflammatory signaling through activation of pathways such as the NLRP3 inflammasome and IL-1β/IL-6 axis. TET2 mutations, in particular, have been consistently linked to diastolic dysfunction and adverse remodeling, especially in patients with high inflammatory burden and cardiometabolic comorbidities. CHIP represents a novel link between ageing, inflammation, and HFpEF, contributing to disease heterogeneity and progression. It may serve as a biomarker for early detection, risk stratification, and patient phenotyping, while also offering potential therapeutic targets. Future research should focus on validating these findings and integrating CHIP into precision medicine approaches for HFpEF.

articles.title: Can radiological parameters predict failure of fixation in distal radius fractures treated with a volar locking plate?
articles.abstract: Fractures of the distal radius are common, and volar locking plates are the most utilized fixation method. Failure of fixation, defined as post-operative fracture collapse leading to loss of reduction and/or screw penetration, is an undesirable outcome. We aimed to demonstrate whether preoperative and intraoperative radiographic parameters are associated with subsequent failure of fixation in order to produce a model that may be able to predict failure. A retrospective case-control study of 23 cases of failure of fixation matched to controls from the same cohort by age, sex, and AO classification in a 3:1 ratio. Nine initial injury and 13 intraoperative radiological parameters were evaluated, and multi-variate regression analysis models were analysed to assess if they could reliably predict failure. A total of 92 patients were analysed (23 cases, 69 controls). Size of intraarticular gap was the only preoperative parameter to be associated failure with every 0.47 mm increase in fracture gap resulting in a 1.6 increase of odds ratio of failure. Based on intraoperative radiological parameters, three factors were associated with failure: dorsal capitate translation, intraarticular gap and step. Models based on these parameters do not accurately predict failure, however, models based on intraoperative factors are associated with risk of failure with high specificity but low sensitivity. We conclude that the severity of the injury is less importantly associated with failure of fixation, whereas the quality of the surgical fixation and specifically the accuracy of the reduction are more important.

articles.title: Trailhead to Triage: A Backcountry Ski Workshop for Sharpening Clinical Decision Making in Emergency Medicine Residents.
articles.abstract: IntroductionDecision making in emergency medicine is influenced by cognitive bias, time pressure, uncertainty, and incomplete or unreliable feedback. Outdoor experiential learning may provide an environment in which these decision-making processes can be experienced and discussed in a practical context.ObjectiveThis study evaluated a novel outdoor experiential learning workshop designed to assess changes in emergency medicine residents' self-reported awareness and understanding of decision-making science.MethodsWe conducted a prospective single-cohort study of emergency medicine residents participating in an outdoor experiential learning workshop. Residents completed a 15-min asynchronous video lecture during the 2 wk preceding the field day, followed by guided backcountry activities incorporating structured discussions of decision-making science and clinical parallels. Participants completed surveys before and after the workshop and a 3-mo follow-up survey. Descriptive statistics and independent-samples t tests were used to evaluate changes in self-reported decision-making awareness and understanding.ResultsThirty residents completed the pre-intervention survey, 21 (70%) completed the post-intervention survey, and 22 (73%) completed the 3-mo follow-up. All measures demonstrated overall improvements from before to after the survey. The largest improvement was in understanding the importance of feedback in decision making (3.53±1.17 vs 4.38±0.74; P=0.001). This improvement maintained statistical significance at the longitudinal follow-up (3.53±1.17 vs 4.09±1.11; P=0.043), reflecting continued appreciation for the value of feedback in decision making.ConclusionsParticipants reported increased awareness and understanding of decision-making science following the workshop, with several measures remaining elevated at the 3-mo follow-up. Participants also reported high levels of enjoyment and perceived educational value.

articles.title: Opportunities for age-friendly emergency care: a mixed-methods study of older adult experiences in a Canadian Emergency Department.
articles.abstract: The aim of this study was to gain insight into the perceptions of care quality and ED experiences of older adults in a Canadian emergency department to develop targeted interventions to improve care experience and outcomes. This study utilized a mixed-methods approach. Semi-structured phone interviews were conducted within 30 days of the index ED visit for 19 consenting participants. Survey data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, while qualitative data from interviews were coded using Nvivo software until thematic saturation was achieved. Surveys were administered to 120 older adults (65 years and older). The majority of older adults surveyed use the ED 2-5 times per year and primarily resided in an urban setting. Survey results identified that older adults were hungry and thirsty during their stay (56.7%), relied on care partners for help during their ED visit (29.2%), and the majority felt heard at triage (93.3%). Interview results identified four major themes and 12 subthemes, highlighting many challenges and opportunities in the care of older adults in the ED. Major themes were communication, care, facilities, and attitudes. While older adults expressed appreciation and general acceptance of current ED conditions, they highlighted several areas needing improvement, including enhanced communication from physicians, better privacy measures, parking accessibility, and improved accommodations for caregivers. This study highlights the unique challenges older adults face in the ED. While many expressed satisfaction and appreciation for their care, key areas for improvement emerged, especially in communication, privacy, and support services. Targeted interventions, such as geriatric friendly infrastructure and multidisciplinary teams, could improve care quality, patient satisfaction, and outcomes for older adults in the ED.

articles.title: Lessons learned while implementing a reusable orthopedic assistive devices recycling program in the pediatric emergency department.
articles.abstract: Lower extremity injuries are a common pediatric emergency presentation that require families to purchase crutches. These may not be affordable for many families, and crutches are often stored or discarded after treatment. There is a need for a solution to reduce the financial burden for families and medical waste. Using Quality Improvement methodology, our group implemented a reusable orthopedic assistive devices recycling program (ROAR) where crutches were dispensed for return and re-use in our pediatric emergency department. Our aim was to dispense 120 pairs, or at least 50% of crutches used in our department at no cost. After collaborative planning, an operational workflow was designed, and the program was launched in April of 2024. To date, 57 pairs of crutches were dispensed to families at no cost. 25 pairs of these crutches were returned at the time of submission. This represents a 44% return rate within the ROAR program. The program was well received by patients and staff, but faced barriers in recuperation of crutches, ultimately limiting its ability to meet our aim and increasing the cost of the program. Valuable progress was made including alleviating some financial strain on families in purchasing medical devices in our emergency department. In future iterations, adoption and staff buy-in should be maximized by emphasizing repeated education for staff, simple documentation and creative replacement of supplies including considering device donations.

articles.title: Emergency physicians' knowledge and practice in reporting medically unfit drivers in Atlantic Canada.
articles.abstract: Emergency physicians frequently encounter patients with medical conditions affecting their fitness to drive. Emergency physicians have legal and ethical duties to report medically unfit drivers. However, many report low confidence in making these decisions. This may lead to underreporting. We aimed to assess knowledge, practice, and barriers regarding reporting of unfit drivers by Atlantic Canadian emergency physicians. We conducted a cross-sectional survey of emergency physicians from four Atlantic Provinces. The survey contained 62 questions across four categories: 1) Demographics (seven), 2) General knowledge (five), 3) Scenarios/practice (34), 4) Barriers/needs (16). Where appropriate, participants rated answers on a five-point Likert scale. Seventy-eight emergency physicians (response rate 20.6%) completed the survey: male (59.0%), age 35-44 (37.2%), formally trained in emergency medicine (74.7%). Overall, 88.5% lacked formal training to determine fitness to drive. Familiarity was low regarding provincial regulations (61.5% "slightly" or "somewhat" familiar) and the Canadian Medical Association Driver's guide (85.9% "not at all" to "somewhat" familiar) while most (80.8%) use clinical judgment to guide decisions. Half indicated they report (56.4%) and document (50.0%) unfit drivers only "sometimes" or less frequently. When presented with clinical scenarios where reporting is indicated (first seizure, recurrent seizure), most (100% and 96.2%) would advise the patients not to drive, but a third (33.4% and 37.2%) would either not report or leave it to another physician to do so. Lack of guideline knowledge was the most significant barrier to reporting, while pocket cards, an electronic app and electronic method to report were identified as enablers. Most emergency physicians (85.9%) would like formal education on this topic. Atlantic Canadian emergency physicians expressed low familiarity with guidelines for determining medical fitness to drive and disclosed potential underreporting. Efforts should focus on targeted education and streamlined tools to improve reporting and enhance road safety.

articles.title: Association between acute GFAP status and 6-month cognitive performance after mild traumatic brain injury: an exploratory follow-up study.
Clinical validation of the DRoPH score: a preoperative tool for estimating reduction difficulty in proximal humerus fractures.
articles.journal: European journal of trauma and emergency surgery : official publication of the European Trauma Society
articles.abstract: Proximal humerus fractures are common injuries that are frequently associated with considerable technical challenges during surgical reduction and fixation. Although anatomical reduction is crucial for fracture healing and functional recovery, the anticipated difficulty of achieving satisfactory reduction is difficult to estimate preoperatively. The Difficulty of Reduction of Proximal Humerus Fractures (DRoPH) score was recently developed through a structured expert consensus process to estimate anticipated reduction difficulty based on predefined fracture- and patient-related characteristics. The aim of this study was to perform an initial clinical validation of the score. We retrospectively analyzed patients who underwent plate fixation of proximal humerus fractures at a tertiary trauma center between January 2014 and December 2024. DRoPH scores (0-10 points) were stratified into low (0-3), moderate (4-6), and high (7-10) difficulty categories. Validation was based on operative duration, postoperative reduction quality according to the criteria described by Schnetzke et al., and postoperative complications. Multivariable regression analyses were performed to assess the independent association of the DRoPH score with the primary outcomes after adjustment for age, sex, and surgical approach. Inter- and intra-rater reliability were assessed using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC). Of 1,012 patients treated for proximal humerus fractures, 392 met the inclusion criteria and had complete datasets available for analysis. Of these, 151 (38.5%) were classified as low, 186 (47.4%) as moderate, and 55 (14.0%) as high difficulty according to the DRoPH score. Operative duration increased significantly with increasing DRoPH scores, with an adjusted increase of 7.3 min per score point (95% CI 5.7-9.0; p < 0.001). Reduction quality deteriorated across difficulty categories, and higher DRoPH scores were independently associated with malreduction (OR 1.30 per point, 95% CI 1.12-1.50; p = 0.001). Overall complication rates increased from 15.2% in low-difficulty fractures to 34.5% in high-difficulty fractures, and the DRoPH score remained independently associated with complications in multivariable analysis (OR 1.15 per point, 95% CI 1.03-1.28; p = 0.012). Inter- and intra-rater reliability of the overall DRoPH score were excellent (ICC 0.96 and 0.95, respectively). This study provides initial clinical validation of the DRoPH score as a reliable and clinically applicable tool for estimating reduction difficulty in proximal humerus fracture fixation. Higher DRoPH scores are independently associated with longer operative duration, increased risk of malreduction, and higher complication rates. The score may therefore serve as a useful adjunct for preoperative planning and risk stratification in surgically treated proximal humerus fractures. Further multicenter validation studies are warranted. Level III, retrospective cohort study.

articles.title: Disaster Report: Military Helicopter Crash in a Deployed Environment - Providers' and Patient's Perspectives.
articles.abstract: The crash of a military helicopter during a 2023 United States Army deployment produced a mass-casualty incident (MASCAL) in an austere setting. One of the casualties was an Emergency Medicine (EM) physician who oversaw point-of-injury (POI) triage and early casualty evacuation with a Special Operations Forces (SOF) medic to the nearest Role II Military Treatment Facility (MTF), followed by movement of the six most severely injured patients to Role III, and subsequent transfer to Landstuhl Regional Medical Center (LRMC) via Critical Care Air Transport Team (CCATT). This disaster report explores the EM physician's actions as the initial provider, another EM physician as a receiving provider for a multi-leg fixed-wing transport, and a practicing trauma surgeon's unique perspective as one of the significantly injured patients. The viewpoints in this report highlight operational decisions including dispersion of medical assets, dynamic triage, destination/platform selection, and significant stressors of flight. Disaster care pathways should anticipate aeromedical stressors, emphasize patient positioning and communication, and align evacuation decisions with changing resources and injury patterns. These lessons are directly relevant to prehospital/disaster systems operating in contested, austere, or resource-limited environments.

articles.title: Association between the site of emergency care and patient-centered outcomes in patients with cancer: rationale and design of the French COVER cohort.
articles.journal: European journal of emergency medicine : official journal of the European Society for Emergency Medicine
articles.abstract: Patients living with cancer now account for a substantial and growing share of emergency department (ED) visits and carry a high burden of hospitalization and in-hospital death. Their acute presentations are frequently multifactorial - driven by disease progression, treatment toxicity, immunosuppression, or the decompensation of comorbid conditions. They may present with higher rates of complications because of novel therapies, such as immune checkpoint inhibitors and cellular therapies, whose emergency manifestations remain unfamiliar to many emergency physicians. Despite this growing importance, the unscheduled care of patients with cancer has received comparatively little dedicated research. How these patients are managed in the ED, how often the emergency physician can access the oncology medical record and goals of care, how the acute complications of new anticancer therapies present, and how a background of cancer should modify the diagnostic approach to everyday emergencies remain poorly characterized. To address these gaps, the Cohort of Onco-hematologic patients visiting the Emergency depaRtment was designed as a prospective, multicenter French cohort of consecutive adults with active cancer or in remission for less than 1 year, presenting to the ED for any reason. Enrollment took place across a national network of 76 EDs for two 1-week periods (summer 2025 and winter 2025-2026), with follow-up to 90 days, yielding a large sample of patients designed as a platform for multiple analyses. The primary aim of Cohort of Onco-hematologic patients visiting the Emergency depaRtment is to determine whether being managed in an ED located within the patient's own cancer referral center, rather than any other hospital, is associated with improvement in morbidity and mortality, captured by the number of days alive and out of hospital at 30 days. Beyond this primary aim, the cohort will support a broad research program on the place of the ED in the cancer care pathway, from patient profiling and pathway description to the emergency toxicities of anticancer drugs and the cancer-specific features of common presentations.

articles.title: Diagnostic Variability in the Modified Kocher Criteria for Septic Arthritis of the Hip: Implications for Aspiration Decision-Making.
articles.abstract: This study evaluates the clinical application of the modified Kocher criteria (MKC) in assessing septic arthritis of the hip (SAH) at a tertiary children's hospital. A retrospective cohort study was conducted on subjects presenting to the emergency department and receiving a hip ultrasound over a 1-year period. Those without a hip effusion were excluded. Patient demographics, symptoms, imaging, labs, treatment, and final diagnoses were collected. SAH was defined clinically by the treating team, supported by patient presentation, lab/imaging findings, operative intervention, and antibiotic therapy. Descriptive and bivariate statistics based on variable distribution were used during analysis. A total of 326 subjects were identified, and 110 had effusion present on ultrasound. Eighteen (16.4%) underwent aspiration. Aspirated subjects had significantly higher cumulative MKC scores (P=0.001) and higher median values for all individual MKC components, including CRP, WBC, ESR, maximum temperature, and a higher prevalence of non-weight-bearing (P<0.05). SAH was diagnosed in 38.9% of the aspirated group (n=7), with MKC scores of 2 (n=2), 3 (n=3), and 5 (n=2). Aspiration rates increased across MKC scores 0 to 3, and synovial fluid inflammatory markers trended higher with increasing MKC scores. Thirteen subjects with an MKC score of 2 were not aspirated; final diagnoses included transient synovitis (n=9), hip effusion, osteomyelitis, sickle cell crisis, or limp (each n=1). Three subjects with an MKC score of 3 were not aspirated and later diagnosed with metastatic tumor, osteomyelitis, and rheumatic fever. Pediatric patients undergoing hip aspiration with a concern for SAH had significantly higher cumulative MKC scores and higher levels of all individual MKC components than their nonaspirated counterparts. However, nearly 15% of patients had MKC scores of 2 or 3 that were not aspirated in the ED, and SAH was identified even in lower-score subjects. While MKC scores appear to influence clinical decision-making, diagnostic variability remains. In patients with intermediate MKC scores of 2 to 3, the criteria should prompt further evaluation, taking into consideration the overall clinical context to guide aspiration decision-making.

articles.title: Similar Presentations, Divergent Clinical Courses: Pediatric Headache Care in the Emergency Department.
articles.abstract: Pediatric emergency department (ED) headache presentations may follow heterogeneous clinical courses. To compare presentation characteristics, migraine order-set activation, pain-score change, treatment intensity, and health care utilization between pediatric ED headache encounters with and without a clinician-documented persistent/intractable headache. We conducted a multisite retrospective cross-sectional study of children aged 3 to 18 years presenting to 2 pediatric EDs with headache or migraine as a chief complaint from 2019 to 2023. Encounters were classified by clinician documentation of an intractable/refractory headache diagnosis or persistent symptoms despite initial treatment. The primary outcome was change from arrival to posttreatment/disposition pain score. Sensitivity analyses were restricted to each patient's first encounter and to clinician-documented migraine or status migrainosus. Among 529 encounters, 18.5% had a documented persistent/intractable headache course. Most presentation characteristics were similar, although symptom duration and pulmonary comorbidity differed. Order-set activation did not differ significantly (76.5% vs. 68.2%; P = 0.106). Encounters with a persistent/intractable headache had less pain improvement [median: -4 (interquartile range: -6.75 to -1) vs. -5 (interquartile range: -7 to -3); P = 0.002], received more medications, radiologic imaging (39.8% vs. 26%; P = 0.006), neurology consultation (56.1% vs. 39.4%; P = 0.003), hospitalization (19.4% vs. 3.2%; P < 0.001), and 30-day return ED visits (10.2% vs. 4.6%; P = 0.049). The pain-score difference was attenuated in the first-encounter analysis (P = 0.060), but persisted in the clinician-documented migraine subgroup (P = 0.006). Headache presentation characteristics and order-set activation did not distinguish the ED course, but pain improvement, treatment intensity, and utilization differed during ED care. Prospective studies should evaluate standardized early reassessment measures.

articles.title: Charting the rise of artificial intelligence in medical education: a global bibliometric and network analysis, 2000-2026.
articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence has moved from a peripheral curiosity to a core feature of modern medical education through adaptive learning, simulation-based training, automated assessment, and large language models such as ChatGPT. Publication activity has accelerated rapidly, but the structure of this expanding literature has not been comprehensively mapped. Bibliographic data were obtained from the Web of Science Core Collection using a search strategy that combined medical education terms in the title field with artificial intelligence terms in the topic field. Articles, review articles, and data papers published from 2000 to 2026 were included. A total of 2,298 records were retrieved. Microsoft Excel was used for descriptive analyses, and VOSviewer (version 1.6.20) was used to construct keyword co-occurrence, country collaboration, and institutional collaboration networks. Data for 2026 represent a partial calendar year. Publication output remained limited until the late 2010s and rose sharply after 2021. Of the 2,298 records, 2,066 (89.9%) were published from 2021 to 2026, with the highest complete-year output in 2025 (821 publications). The United States led in publication volume (918 records) and raw citation count (14,582 citations), followed by the People's Republic of China (367 records; 4,404 citations). The Journal of Surgical Education published the most articles. Harvard Medical School led institutional output, whereas Stanford University and the University of California San Francisco had higher raw citation totals despite fewer publications. Artificial intelligence, medical education, ChatGPT, medical students, and machine learning were the most prominent keywords. Artificial intelligence in medical education is a rapidly expanding but geographically and institutionally concentrated field. Raw citation patterns differed from publication volume, although these unadjusted measures should not be interpreted as direct comparisons of research quality. Thematic patterns emphasize learner-facing applications, assessment, and generative AI, while responsible curricular integration and empirical evaluation remain important priorities. These findings are especially relevant to emergency medicine education, where simulation, time-sensitive decision-making, and competency assessment are central.

articles.title: Assessing MRI utility in pediatric tibial-sided PCL avulsion fractures: the reference standard matters.
Impact of Structured Preoperative Counseling on Anaesthesia Preference in Elective Cesarean Delivery: A Prospective Study.
articles.journal: Turkish journal of anaesthesiology and reanimation
articles.abstract: To assess changes in anaesthesia preference before and after structured preoperative counseling and to identify factors associated with anaesthesia preference among women scheduled for elective cesarean delivery. This prospective, single-center, single-arm, pre-post observational study included 200 pregnant women classified as the American Society of Anesthesiologists physical status II. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire assessing demographic characteristics, obstetric history, previous anaesthesia experience, level of knowledge, and anaesthesia preference, both before and after counseling. Statistical analyses were performed using SPSS version 22.0, and a P value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. At baseline, 53% of patients preferred spinal anaesthesia and 47% preferred general anaesthesia. Following counseling, the preference for spinal anaesthesia increased to 88.5% (P < 0.001). Increasing age was associated with a decreased likelihood of choosing spinal anaesthesia [odds ratio (OR)=0.94, 95% confidence interval (CI): 0.89-0.99], whereas higher education (OR=1.78, 95% CI: 1.05-3.02), prior knowledge (OR=1.65, 95% CI: 1.02-2.68), and previous spinal anaesthesia experience (OR=2.95, 95% CI: 1.65-5.28) were identified as independent predictors of spinal anaesthesia preference. No significant association was found between smoking and anaesthesia preference, or between comorbidities and anaesthesia preference. The postoperative satisfaction rate with the anaesthesia was 91.5%. Following structured preoperative counseling, the preference for neuraxial anaesthesia increased among women scheduled for elective cesarean delivery. These findings suggest that standardized patient education may be a useful component of preoperative anaesthesia assessment.

articles.title: Interpreting the 42% displacement threshold in pediatric proximal humerus fractures: age still matters.
Reply to: Interpreting the 42% displacement threshold in pediatric proximal humerus fractures: age still matters.
Hybrid Airway Management for Neuromonitoring-guided Selective Phrenic Nerve Surgery in Intractable Hiccups: A Case Report.
articles.journal: Turkish journal of anaesthesiology and reanimation
articles.abstract: Intractable hiccups are rare but debilitating, and may cause sleep disturbances, nutritional impairment, exhaustion, and a severe deterioration in quality of life. When pharmacological and interventional treatments fail, selected surgical procedures targeting the phrenic nerve may be considered. We report the anaesthetic management of a 32-year-old woman with idiopathic intractable hiccups who underwent right-sided selective phrenic nerve surgery guided by thoracoscopic neuromonitoring. Because thoracoscopic exposure and intraoperative neuromonitoring were required simultaneously, a hybrid airway strategy combining an electromyography endotracheal tube with a bronchial blocker was used. The patient was positioned in the left lateral decubitus position, and the bronchial blocker was placed in the right main bronchus under fiberoptic bronchoscopic guidance. One-lung ventilation was maintained for 35 minutes with FiO2 of 0.70 to 0.80, tidal volume of 5-6 mL kg-1, respiratory rate of 18 min-1, and PEEP of 5 cmH2O; the arterial blood gas analysis at 25 minutes showed pH 7.38, PaCO2 41 mmHg, and PaO2 92 mmHg. Sugammadex was administered intraoperatively to restore diaphragmatic motor responses required for branch-specific neuromonitoring. The medial and anterolateral branches of the right phrenic nerve exhibited abnormal electrophysiological responses and were treated with selective bipolar ablation and clipping. Postoperatively, the patient remained on room air, reported no intraoperative recall, and showed no clinically relevant diaphragmatic dysfunction on clinical and functional assessment. This case illustrates that established anaesthetic techniques can be carefully adapted to meet the competing requirements of lung isolation, anaesthetic depth control, and neuromonitoring in selected patients undergoing phrenic nerve surgery for intractable hiccups.

articles.title: Comparison of Postoperative Analgesic Efficacy Between Opioid-free Anaesthesia Using Intravenous Magnesium, Lidocaine, and Erector Spinae Plane Block, and Opioid-based Anaesthesia in Laparoscopic Abdominal Surgeries: A Randomised Controlled Trial.
articles.journal: Turkish journal of anaesthesiology and reanimation
articles.abstract: Opioid-based anaesthesia is a standard practice in laparoscopic surgeries. However, it is associated with adverse effects that can limit its use. To address these issues, opioid-free anaesthesia has been introduced as an alternative. This study aims to compare the analgesic efficacy of opioid-free anaesthesia, incorporating magnesium, lidocaine, and an erector spinae plane block (ESPB), with traditional opioid-based anaesthesia during laparoscopic procedures. Seventy patients aged 18-60 years undergoing laparoscopic surgery were randomly divided into two groups of 35 each. Opioid-free group received opioid-free anaesthesia, which included an intravenous (IV) bolus of 2 g magnesium, a continuous lidocaine infusion at 1.5 mg kg-1 hr-1, and a bilateral ESPB with 25 mL of 0.25% bupivacaine. Opioid-based group received opioid-based anaesthesia with an IV dose of 2 μg kg-1 fentanyl. Postoperative pain and the need for rescue analgesia were assessed for 24 h. Perioperative haemodynamic parameters were recorded, and the incidence of postoperative complications, including sedation, nausea, vomiting, and shivering, was monitored for 24 h. Pain scores were significantly lower in the opioid-free group compared to the opioid-based group at 0 h (P < 0.001), 2 h (P < 0.001), and 4 h (P=0.005) postoperatively. The opioid-based group required rescue analgesia more frequently (P < 0.001). Additionally, the incidence of postoperative complications was significantly lower in the opioid-free group than in the opioid-based group (P < 0.001). Haemodynamic parameters were similar between the two groups. Opioid-free anaesthesia provides superior postoperative analgesia and reduces the incidence of postoperative complications compared with opioid-based anaesthesia for laparoscopic surgery.

articles.title: Harnessing the Power of Education for a Low-carbon Future in Anaesthesia: A Narrative Review.
articles.journal: Turkish journal of anaesthesiology and reanimation
articles.abstract: Climate change poses a significant threat to public health, with the healthcare sector being a major contributor to greenhouse gas emissions. Anaesthesia and the operating room are notable contributors within this sector, particularly because of volatile inhalation gases such as desflurane and nitrous oxide. Therefore, improving sustainability in anaesthesia is a clinical and ethical imperative. This review examines recent advances in leveraging education to promote low-carbon anaesthesia practices. We summarize evidence on how various educational interventions and formats can reduce the carbon footprint of anaesthesia and discuss implementation strategies, challenges, and future directions. Many studies demonstrate that educational programs reduce the use of high global warming potential anaesthetic agents. Programs vary widely in scope, ranging from single-session lectures and surveys to multi-year sustainability task forces and formal policy changes, some of which have resulted in up to a 90% reduction in volatile agent emissions. Combining multiple techniques (such as lectures, posters, and vaporizer labeling) has been associated with substantial reductions in volatile agent emissions and with improved organizational readiness for sustainability initiatives. These education-driven shifts toward environmentally friendly approaches, such as low-flow techniques, total intravenous anaesthesia, and regional anaesthesia, have proven effective, cutting costs, maintaining patient safety, and reducing carbon emissions. Educational initiatives represent a practical and cost‑efficient strategy to reduce carbon emissions in anaesthesia practice and in healthcare. By integrating environmental stewardship into anaesthesia training and policy, anaesthesiologists can lead the transition of healthcare to low-carbon care.

articles.title: The Analgesia Nociception Index is More Strongly Associated with Anxiety Than with Pain in Conscious Male Patients Undergoing Hernia Repair Under Combined Spinal-epidural Anaesthesia.
articles.journal: Turkish journal of anaesthesiology and reanimation
articles.abstract: The Analgesia Nociception Index (ANI), derived from heart rate variability, is a non-invasive marker of the nociception- analgesia balance. Its validity and validity in conscious are uncertain because activity may also psychological factors, particularly anxiety. This exploratory study examined the among ANI, pain, and anxiety in male patients undergoing hernia repair with combined spinal-epidural anaesthesia (CSEA). Twenty-four male patients with American Society of Anesthesiologists physical status I-II undergoing hernia repair under CSEA were enrolled. Self-reported visual analogue scale for Anxiety (VAS-A), pain (VAS), and continuously recorded ANI were assessed at four procedural stages: lateral positioning (T1), local anaesthetic infiltration (T2), epidural puncture (T3), and two minutes post-puncture (T4). Within-patient (primary), patient-level, and observation-level correlations were and the two within-patient correlations involving ANI were formally compared. At the within-patient level, ANI correlated negatively with anxiety (r=-0.794, P < 0.001) and with pain (r=-0.515, P < 0.001); the ANI-stronger than the ANI-pain correlation. The association between ANI and anxiety was significantly stronger than that between ANI and pain (Hotelling-Williams t=4.10, P < 0.001). The patient-level ANI--pain analysis was clearly underpowered (post-hoc power ≈ 0.18). Clinicians should therefore avoid interpreting a low ANI value as evidence of inadequate analgesia alone and should consider concurrent assessment of both pain and anxiety. These findings should be regarded as hypothesis-generating and require confirmation in larger, sex-balanced, multicentre studies. Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05053633), registered 22 September 2021.

articles.title: Low-Angle Paramedian Approach versus Midline Approach for Remote Access Epidural Blood Patch: A Case Report.
articles.journal: Turkish journal of anaesthesiology and reanimation
articles.abstract: While mid-thoracic CSF leaks (T7-T8) require targeted epidural blood patches, direct thoracic puncture carries a significant risk of spinal cord injury due to the narrow epidural space. To mitigate this risk, a safety-oriented remote-access strategy from the T12-L1 level, with cranial advancement of the catheter, was employed to prevent direct thoracic spinal cord injury. We present a 46-year-old male with a T7-T8 leak in whom a standard midline approach failed due to poor catheter steerability. By adopting a low-angle (<30°) paramedian approach, we achieved precise ipsilateral catheter positioning; this technical modification provides optimized vector alignment and a tangential epidural trajectory for unilateral thoracic leaks. This technical modification may improve maneuverability and safety for unilateral thoracic leaks, compared to standard midline techniques, and appears to facilitate an optimized tangential trajectory in this case.

articles.title: Trends in the Use of Neuraxial vs. General Anaesthesia for Transurethral Resection of the Prostate.
articles.journal: Turkish journal of anaesthesiology and reanimation
articles.abstract: Historically, neuraxial anaesthesia (NA) was preferred for transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP) to allow monitoring for TURP syndrome, but modern surgical techniques have largely eliminated this risk. We aimed to characterise trends in anaesthesia utilisation for TURP over a 15-year period and to identify patient factors associated with anaesthetic technique selection. We performed a retrospective cohort study of patients undergoing primary TURP using the ACS-NSQIP database (2009-2023). Multivariable logistic regression identified predictors of the use of general anaesthesia (GA) versus NA. Subgroup analyses examined trends by patient health status and age. Of 73,214 patients identified, GA utilisation increased significantly from 69.9% in 2009 to 88.8% in 2023 (P < 0.001). In multivariable analysis, each successive year was associated with a 15% increase in the odds of receiving GA [odds ratio (OR) 1.15, 95% confidence interval (CI) 1.14-1.15]. Black patients (OR 1.65, 95% CI 1.47-1.87) had higher odds of GA than white patients, and hispanic patients (OR 1.51, 95% CI 1.38-1.64) had higher odds of GA than non-hispanic patients. Conversely, older age, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (OR 0.77, 95% CI 0.71-0.84), and diabetes (OR 0.88, 95% CI 0.84-0.93) were associated with decreased GA use. The shift towards GA was significantly more pronounced among medically complex patients (American Society of Anesthesiologists 3-4) than among less medically complex patients (P=0.005). The anaesthetic management of TURP has evolved over the last 15 years, and GA has further solidified its status as the dominant modality. This evolution likely reflects the diminished risk of TURP syndrome, allowing practice to be driven by airway control and efficiency rather than by historical safety constraints.

articles.title: One-Lung Ventilation for Neonatal Pneumonectomy in a Hydropic Premature Infant: Fiberoptic-guided Left Mainstem Intubation.
articles.journal: Turkish journal of anaesthesiology and reanimation
articles.abstract: Congenital cystic adenomatoid malformation (CCAM) is a rare lung anomaly that can cause severe respiratory distress and hydrops fetalis. One-lung ventilation (OLV) in neonates poses extreme anatomical challenges due to the lack of appropriately sized double-lumen tubes or bronchial blockers. A male neonate (2500 g, 30 weeks' gestation) presented with hydrops fetalis and a massive right-sided thoracic CCAM. Due to progressive respiratory failure and hemodynamic instability, an emergency right pneumonectomy was scheduled on postnatal day 3. To achieve OLV, a 3.5-mm cuffed endotracheal tube (with the cuff left deflated) was advanced into the left main bronchus under fiberoptic bronchoscopy (FOB) guidance. Removal of the tube adaptor facilitated rapid, pragmatic placement while minimizing interruptions to ventilation during apneic oxygenation. Pressure-controlled lung-protective ventilation was maintained. Transient desaturation episodes during mediastinal manipulation were successfully managed. The 3-hour procedure was completed without intraoperative complications. In premature neonates in whom commercial lung-isolation devices are impractical, FOB-guided selective mainstem bronchial intubation is a rapid, feasible, and effective strategy for OLV. Individualized airway planning and FOB guidance are instrumental in ensuring accurate placement and maintaining oxygenation.

articles.title: Adaptability of Medical Surge Preparedness Practices to Large-Scale Combat Operations.
articles.abstract: Since its inception, the National Disaster Medical System (NDMS) has been activated in the context of acute-onset and time-limited disasters; however, its original intended purpose was for providing care for casualties from a large-scale combat operation (LSCO). Consequently, determining the utility of specific medical surge practices for an LSCO is necessary to optimally prepare the NDMS for such an event. Lessons learned from prior medical surge events can inform LSCO preparations despite the contextual differences between the 2 scenarios. This case study builds on earlier analyses by the US Department of Defense's NDMS Pilot program to develop a set of evidence-based leading practices for improving medical surge response that can be used by healthcare facilities providing acute care during LSCO-related patient surges.

articles.title: Ultra-high-resolution photon-counting CT argues against a suspected bilateral carotid web: a case report.
articles.abstract: Carotid web is diagnosed almost entirely from a shelf-like filling defect at CT angiography (CTA), yet the posterolateral carotid bulb at which webs arise is also a site of flow separation in which blood of differing contrast density mixes. We describe a bilateral web-like appearance at this site and determine whether it arose from reconstruction or acquisition. A 75-year-old woman with a right-hemispheric transient ischemic attack had three carotid CTA examinations: a dual-energy energy-integrating-detector CT (EID-CT) angiogram five months before presentation, a stroke-protocol photon-counting-detector CT (PCD-CT) angiogram at presentation, and a dedicated ultra-high-resolution PCD-CT angiogram three days later. Each photon-counting acquisition was additionally reconstructed with other section thicknesses, kernels or energies, and attenuation across the appearance was measured. A bilateral shelf-like filling defect closely simulating a carotid web was present on the EID-CT and presenting PCD-CTF angiograms but absent on the ultra-high-resolution study. The tested reconstructions neither abolished the appearance nor elicited it. The ultra-high-resolution study was acquired 16.6 s after the end of injection at less than half the table speed, versus 10.3 s on the presenting study. Attenuation at the corresponding position measured 62%, 54% and 87% of luminal attenuation, respectively. No carotid intervention was undertaken. An acquisition-dependent bilateral carotid bulb pseudolesion can mimic a carotid web on both EID-CT and PCD-CT angiography and is most consistent with flow-related mixing of blood of differing contrast density. A slower repeat acquisition of the carotid bulb with a few seconds more delay may prevent unnecessary revascularization.

articles.title: A narrative review of CBRN health sector preparedness in Lebanon.
articles.abstract: As chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear (CBRN) events become increasingly recognised within international and national emergency preparedness efforts, this study aims to provide the first system-level overview of Lebanon's preparedness capacities for CBRN-related health emergencies. A narrative review of peer-reviewed and grey literature was conducted using a structured search strategy, with findings thematically synthesised to assess governance and operational CBRN preparedness capacities across eight health system domains in Lebanon. The review identified important advances in Lebanon's preparedness for CBRN health emergencies, including engagement with international preparedness frameworks, development of governance structures, and implementation of coordination, training, and simulation initiatives. However, preparedness remains uneven and constrained by fragmented coordination, legislative gaps, limited surveillance and operational integration, shortages in material and human resources, and dependence on external support. Economic instability and workforce migration further challenge sustainability, while preparedness capacities and readiness levels vary across emergency response and healthcare institutions. Overall, strategic planning and governance capacities appeared stronger than operational response and surveillance functions. While major efforts towards CBRN preparedness in Lebanon have been initiated, key aspects remain under-developed. Given Lebanon's continued exposure to recurrent crises and regional instability, strengthening CBRN preparedness should be considered a critical component of broader health system resilience and national disaster risk reduction efforts.

articles.title: Development and independent regional validation of a dynamic ultrasound appendicitis score for suspected acute appendicitis: a prospective multicenter study.
articles.abstract: Acute appendicitis is the most common surgical emergency. Although CT is highly accurate, radiation exposure is a major concern in children, young adults, and pregnant women. Ultrasound is radiation-free but operator-dependent, and current scores rely on static weights without accounting for important patient-finding interactions. To develop and independently validate a Dynamic Ultrasound Appendicitis Score (Dynamic UAS) with interaction effects to improve risk stratification and potentially avoid unnecessary CT examinations. A prospective multicenter study collected development (n = 802) and independent regional external validation (n = 262) data. The Dynamic UAS was derived using multivariable logistic regression with interaction terms and internally validated using bootstrapping (1000 resamples). A web-based calculator was developed. A sensitivity analysis addressed limitations of the reference standard, non-visualized appendix, and missing data. Appendicitis prevalence was 33.3% (development) and 32.8% (validation). The Dynamic UAS performed excellently in diagnosing acute appendicitis (AUC 0.96 and 0.94) and outperformed known scores (AUC 0.81 to 0.91). At the ≥ 6 level, sensitivity was 91.7%/90.7%, and specificity was 97.1%/96.0%. Calibration was good (slope 0.89, Brier 0.098). In non-visualized appendix cases, the AUC was 0.89 (95% CI: 0.84 to 0.93) in the external validation cohort and 0.90 (95% CI: 0.85 to 0.94) in the development cohort. The model is not very useful for distinguishing complicated from uncomplicated appendicitis (AUC 0.72). The Dynamic UAS is a novel, independently validated tool that may reduce unnecessary CT use in radiation-sensitive populations and resource-limited settings. Future studies in different international settings are needed.

articles.title: Comparison of Acute Physiology, Age and Chronic Health Evaluation II score and Peradeniya Organophosphorus Poisoning Scale in predicting clinical outcomes and mortality in organophosphorus poisoning.
articles.abstract: Organophosphorus poisoning is a major health hazard in developing countries. We conducted a study to compare the Acute Physiology, Age and Chronic Health Evaluation II (APACHE II) scoring system and Peradeniya Organophosphorus Poisoning Scale in predicting the complications, ventilator requirement and mortality in patients of Acute Organophosphorus Poisoning. A prospective observational study was done on 100 patients above 18 years of age, presenting with alleged history of consumption of organophosphorus compounds. The patients were evaluated for the required details to calculate the APACHE II score and Peradeniya Organophosphorus Poisoning Scale and were followed up till discharge or mortality to identify the complications, ventilator requirement and mortality. This data was tabulated using Excel and analyzed using SPSS software to look for correlation between the scores and the outcome. The mean age of our patients was 33.64 ± 12.99 years. The APACHE II cutoff score for complications, ventilator requirement and mortality was ≥ 7 (sensitivity 94.3%, specificity 96.9%, Area under Receiver Operator Characteristic (ROC) 0.99, p < 0.01), ≥9 (sensitivity 86.7%, specificity 82.4%, Area under ROC 0.91, p < 0.01) and ≥16 (sensitivity 85.7, specificity 96.8%, Area under ROC 0.98, p < 0.01) respectively. Similarly, the Peradeniya Organophosphorus Poisoning Scale cutoff was for complications, ventilator requirement and mortality was ≥ 3 (sensitivity 80%, specificity 92.3%, Area under ROC 0.90, p < 0.01), ≥3 (sensitivity 80%, specificity 75.3%, Area under ROC 0.85, p < 0.01) and ≥7 (sensitivity 85.7%, specificity 97.8%, Area under ROC 0.99, p < 0.01) respectively. Both APACHE II and POPS demonstrated good predictive performance for adverse outcomes in acute organophosphorus poisoning. Both scores showed excellent discrimination for mortality, with no statistically significant difference between their AUCs.

articles.title: Psychometric evaluation of the Persian version of the shared decision‑making questionnaire in patients undergoing emergency surgery.
articles.abstract: Accurate assessment of shared decision-making (SDM) is essential in emergency surgery, yet no culturally adapted and validated instrument is available in Iran. This study aimed to translate, culturally adapt, and assess the psychometric properties of the Persian SDM-Q-9 among patients undergoing emergency surgery. This methodological cross-sectional study followed a forward-backward translation procedure to adapt the SDM-Q-9 into Persian. Face and content validity were established prior to construct validation. Data were collected from 575 patients undergoing emergency surgery and randomly split into two independent subsamples for exploratory factor analysis (EFA; n = 287) and confirmatory factor analysis (CFA; n = 288). Internal consistency was assessed using Cronbach's alpha, McDonald's omega, and composite reliability (CR). Convergent validity was examined using average variance extracted (AVE). The data were suitable for factor analysis (Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin [KMO] = 0.923; Bartlett's test of sphericity: χ² = 3433.445, df = 36, p < 0.001). EFA using Maximum Likelihood (ML) extraction with Promax rotation supported a single-factor structure explaining 58.60% of the total variance, with all factor loadings exceeding 0.70. CFA of the independent validation subsample initially showed inadequate fit for the one-factor model. After reviewing modification indices and item content, three theoretically justified residual correlations were retained. The resulting model showed good fit (χ²/df = 2.78, Comparative Fit Index [CFI] = 0.962, Tucker-Lewis Index [TLI] = 0.944, Root Mean Square Error of Approximation [RMSEA] = 0.059, and Standardized Root Mean Square Residual [SRMR] = 0.052). Factor loadings ranged from 0.67 to 0.84, supporting a predominantly unidimensional structure. The scale demonstrated strong internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha = 0.921, McDonald's omega = 0.926, and CR = 0.924). Convergent validity was supported by an AVE of 0.576. The Persian SDM-Q-9 demonstrated satisfactory validity and strong reliability for assessing patient-perceived shared decision-making in emergency surgical settings in Iran. Its predominantly unidimensional structure supports its use, although the localized residual associations identified in CFA warrant replication in independent, multicenter samples.

articles.title: Three doors, three locks: a domain-specific framework for the residual door-to-balloon gap in STEMI care : Matters Arising, commentary on Krishnan et al., Int J Emerg Med 2026;19:113.
articles.abstract: Krishnan and colleagues report that 91% of STEMI patients at a large Indian tertiary centre received primary PCI within the 90-minute door-to-balloon (D2B) target, a meaningful achievement in contemporary STEMI care. Their analysis of the 9% who missed the target is equally valuable: delays distributed almost evenly across three categories, delayed informed consent, hemodynamic instability, and diagnostic ambiguity. We argue these categories are not interchangeable quality-improvement targets. They are mechanistically distinct problems requiring different solutions. We propose a conceptual, hypothesis-generating framework rather than a validated taxonomy. Future STEMI quality improvement efforts should categorize residual delays by domain rather than reporting them in aggregate, and should match interventions to the specific mechanism of delay.
